explain ssh
SSH,
or
Secure
Shell
,
is
a
protocol
for
logging
in
to
another
computer
over
a
network
you
do
not
trust
and
working
on
it
as
if
you
were
at
its
keyboard.
Everything
that
passes
between
the
two
machines
(commands,
output,
files)
is
encrypted
before
it
leaves
and
decrypted
only
on
the
other
end.
###
1.
What
is
it
used
for?
-
Remote
administration:
open
a
shell
on
a
server
to
install
packages,
edit
configs,
or
read
logs.
-
File
transfer:
scp
and
sftp
ride
on
top
of
SSH,
so
copies
inherit
the
same
protection.
-
Port
forwarding:
wrap
a
plaintext
service,
like
a
database
port,
inside
the
tunnel.
###
2.
Where
does
the
security
come
from?
SSH
replaced
Telnet
,
which
sent
passwords
in
the
clear.
It
layers
three
kinds
of
cryptography:
-
Key
exchange:
both
sides
derive
a
fresh
session
key;
an
observer
never
sees
it.
-
Symmetric
encryption:
that
key
encrypts
the
traffic,
fast
enough
for
interactive
use.
-
Integrity
checks:
every
packet
carries
a
MAC,
so
tampering
is
detected
and
the
connection
drops.
###
3.
Keys
instead
of
passwords
Put
your
public
key
on
the
server
in
authorized_keys
.
Your
private
key
never
leaves
your
machine,
so
there
is
no
password
to
phish,
and
access
is
revoked
by
deleting
one
line.
###
4.
A
minimal
config
```
#
~/.ssh/config
Host
prod
HostName
203.0.113.7
User
admin
IdentityFile
~/.ssh/id_ed25519
ForwardAgent
no
```
Then
ssh
prod
connects.
On
the
first
connection
SSH
shows
the
host
fingerprint
and
asks
whether
to
trust
it.
